rationale:
bugs_open/390, commit 2 of 3 - the durable half. Commit 1 (migration 616, applied 2026-08-25) corrected a prompt that was instructing the losing move; this makes the platform MEASURE what the repair must beat instead of guessing.

THE DEFECT. `write_render_audit_findings` files every `contrast_failure` with `handlerAgent: "css-patch-agent"` (a hardcoded literal at :414 - there is no item_type->agent table). That agent APPENDS a rule to the site theme stylesheet. Nothing in the platform knows whether the theme can govern the pixel, and structurally it usually cannot: the winning declaration lives in a per-page <style> block in `page_components.rendered_html`, and `assemblePage` emits those inside <main>, always after the <link> in <head>. So the theme is always earlier in source order, on every page, by construction.

[MEASURED 2026-08-25] 40 random completed findings with real selectors across 7 sites, served page and served theme fetched per finding: the winning `color` declaration was in the page block AND out-specified the filed selector in 33, in the page block at lower specificity in 6, in the theme in 0, not located in 1. Near-uniform shape: filed `TAG.class` (0,1,1) against page `.section .class` (0,2,0). Damage over live UNION archive: 75 of 151 real-selector pairings that ever reached `complete` were filed again; 97 re-filings byte-identical in fg AND bg. At the artefact: noted.co.uk holds 16 appended contrast fixes for 5 distinct selectors.

THE CHANGE, in three parts.

(1) BROWSER. A probe-local JS const (NOT added to the shared contrastMathsJS kernel, which is byte-identical to the string the contrast_ratio check also runs) attributes the declaration that decides `color` for an element already measured as failing: walks document.styleSheets with each .cssRules access in try/catch so a cross-origin sheet counts as opaque instead of aborting, re-evaluates @media/@supports conditions rather than assuming they apply, splits selector lists and records the PART that matched, and includes the element's own style attribute and per-property importance.

(2) THE PROOF, which is the load-bearing idea and the reason this is not just another walker. A walker cannot see everything - cascade layers, an opaque sheet, a duplicate declaration - and a confident wrong answer here is worse than none because a router acts on it. So the walker's ordering is NOT the claim. The probe REMOVES the declaration it believes wins and re-reads the computed value: REMOVING A LOSING DECLARATION CANNOT CHANGE THE COMPUTED VALUE, so if the value moves, the removed declaration WAS the winner. That is sound whatever heuristic chose the candidate, which is exactly why the in-page specificity guess is allowed to be rough - it only decides what to TRY FIRST, and candidates are tried best-first until one moves the value. It UNDER-CLAIMS by construction: when winner and runner-up specify the same value, removal changes nothing and the result is verified:false. Every removal is restored and the restore is CHECKED; a restore that does not take latches the page dirty and attribution stops there (a later measurement would be measuring our own edit). The page instance is discarded after auditOne, so nothing reaches a user.

(3) CHASSIS. A pure function maps the attributed facts to `spec.repair_surface` (theme / unreachable / unattributed) and `spec.override_requirement` (min_specificity, strictly_greater, needs_important, plus an override_example the platform has CHECKED with satisfiesRequirement rather than one it hopes is right). Specificity is computed HERE with cascadia - already a direct dependency - not in the browser, so there is one authority and no second implementation to drift. Only one class is genuinely unreachable by any stylesheet rule: an !important inline style attribute.

FOUR THINGS I DELIBERATELY DID NOT DO, each of which a reviewer should check I held to:

* The `item_key` does NOT change. VIZ-016 records that the key embeds the selector and that changing it already forced two alias-key retrofits in the retraction path. Every new fact rides the spec, and a test pins the key byte-identical with and without attribution.
* `handler_agent` does NOT change, for any route including `unreachable`. Re-routing is a separate decision with its own blast radius; this commit measures and records, it does not redirect. The park for `unreachable` is commit 3, in the agent workflow, so the row keeps its ledger entry and its dedup slot.
* `retractResolvedContrastFindings` is untouched.
* Nothing is written when the adapter does not declare `cascade_scheme`. The spec is then byte-identical to today's, so version skew in either direction degrades to current behaviour rather than to a half-populated new shape.

FOREGROUND ONLY, stated as a boundary rather than left as an oversight: attributing the effective BACKGROUND needs the node effBG stopped at, which is inside the shared kernel.

EIGHT GUARDS MUTATION-PROVEN, each reverted to its plausible-but-wrong form with the named test confirmed RED and the file then diffed byte-identical.

plan.summary: Record what a contrast repair must BEAT, and prove the attribution in the page by removing the declaration and watching the computed value move. plan.risks:
1) EXPECTED OBJECTION - 'this measures but does not fix anything.' Correct, and deliberate. Commit 3 consumes the requirement in the agent's prompt and parks the unreachable class; this commit is inert until both images roll and then only writes spec fields. Splitting them is what keeps the browser change reviewable on its own and lets the routing be checked against real filed rows before anything acts on it.

2) THE BIGGEST REAL RISK - the probe MUTATES the live DOM (removeProperty/setProperty) to prove its answer. Mitigations, in order: every removal is restored and the restore is re-CHECKED against the pre-removal computed value; a failed restore latches window.__cascadeDirty and no further attribution happens on that page; the page instance is discarded after auditOne and is never served to anyone; and the dirty-page count is reported so an occurrence is visible rather than silent. A reviewer should push on whether a failed restore can corrupt the SAME page's remaining contrast measurements - it can, which is exactly why the latch stops attribution rather than merely logging.

3) TIMEOUT BUDGET. Attribution is per-failing-element CSSOM work with no extra navigation, on an adapter already observed running near ~3 minutes. Capped at 40 findings per page with cascade_capped counted. If a timeout regression appears after the roll, this is a candidate - but do not attribute it here without evidence, because the pre-existing budget pressure is unfiled and predates this change.

4) THE ROUGH IN-PAGE SPECIFICITY HEURISTIC is not CSS3-correct (it does not handle :not()/:is() internals or escapes). That is tolerable ONLY because it selects what to try first and never becomes the recorded requirement - cascadia computes that on the chassis, and a selector cascadia cannot parse downgrades the whole finding to unattributed. If a reviewer thinks the heuristic's errors can leak into the output, that is the thing to check, and it is the assumption I would most want challenged.

5) HAND-KEPT MIRROR. cascadeWinner on the chassis is a copy of a struct in another module that rolls in another image; a field added there and forgotten here decodes to its zero value and reads as an older adapter. The parity test with an all-non-zero literal is the only thing turning that silence into a failure - it must be updated in the same commit as any field.

6) COUNTERS WITH NO READER - cascade_attributed/unattributed/unreachable live in the result map and the log line only, the same standing gap as skipped_unverified_selector. Stated in the register entry rather than hidden.

7) OTHER LANES. bugs_open/296 and bugs_open/211 consume contrast_failure rows; the spec change is purely additive and gated, but per the 2026-07-29 ruling they should be TOLD, not merely measured against. write_render_audit_findings_action.go was clean when this landed but is a file three lanes have touched this week.
